title.en: Aoibhell and Dubhlaing's Choice at Cluantarbh
title.zh: 艾薇爾與杜夫萊因在克魯安塔之抉擇

region.en: Craig Liath (The Grey Rock), Co. Tipperary, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭蒂珀雷里郡灰岩（象徵定位）

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. VI, eBook #14465

summary.en: Aoibhell, a woman of the Sidhe dwelling in Craig Liath, loves the young Munsterman Dubhlaing ua Artigan. Before the battle of Cluantarbh she tries to hold him back and wraps him in a Druid covering so no one can see him; refusing to fight unseen, he casts it off. She offers him two hundred years of happy life if he will leave the battle, but he will not give up his king or his good name, and both men fall as she foretold.
summary.zh: 仙族女子艾薇爾居灰岩，愛上年輕的芒斯特戰士杜夫萊因。克魯安塔之戰前她欲留他，並施德魯伊隱形罩使其不可見；杜夫萊因拒絕隱身作戰而卸去罩衣。她許諾二百年歡愉歲月勸其離戰，他不願捨君王與名譽；戰場上二人皆亡，如其所言。

sensitivity.note: A fairy-mistress offering otherworld longevity against heroic fame — the Irish inverse of Achilles' choice. Cluantarbh (Slog in an Elum?) battle located symbolically at traditional Craig Liath site.

passages.text: Aoibhell, another woman of the Sidhe, made her dwelling-place in Craig Liath, and at the time of the battle of Cluantarbh she set her love on a young man of Munster, Dubhlaing ua Artigan, that had been sent away in disgrace by the King of Ireland. But before the battle he came back to join with Murchadh, the king's son, and to fight for the Gael. Aoibhell came to stop him; and when he would not stop with her she put a Druid covering about him, so that no one could see him. He went where Murchadh was fighting, and made a great attack on the enemies of Ireland, striking them down on every side. Murchadh looked around him: "It seems to me I hear the sound of the blows of Dubhlaing ua Artigan, but I do not see himself." Then Dubhlaing threw off the Druid covering: "I will not keep this covering upon me when you cannot see me through it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VI; not verbatim.

passages.text: So they went where Aoibhell was, and she bade them both quit the battle, for they would lose their lives in it. Murchadh said to her: "I will tell you a little true story: that fear for my own body will never make me change my face. And if we fall, the strangers will fall with us." "Stop with me, Dubhlaing," she said, "and you will have two hundred years of happy life with myself." "I will not give up Murchadh," he said, "or my own good name, for silver or gold." There was anger on Aoibhell, and she said: "Murchadh will fall, and you yourself will fall, and your proud blood will be on the plain to-morrow." They went back into the battle, and got their death there.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VI; not verbatim.

region.en: Island of Falga / Emain Ablach (Isle of Man, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 法爾加島／埃曼·阿布拉赫（象徵定位於曼島）

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. VIII, eBook #14465

summary.en: Manannan son of Lir, the sea-god and master of enchantments, is said to have died in battle and been buried standing, where a lake burst up under his feet; yet he was long heard of in Ireland. He raised the sons of Usnach's blindness, was perhaps Culain the Smith, and at the Island of Falga Conchobar bound the sea-queen Tiabhal, whose likeness on the smith's shield lessened the strength of enemies in every battle. His hounds that hunted a destroying pig were all destroyed at the lake called after them, Loch Conn.
summary.zh: 海神瑪那南精通幻術，傳說戰死後立而葬之，腳下湧出湖泊；然其後久聞於愛爾蘭。他使烏斯納克諸子盲目互殘，或謂鐵匠庫蘭即其化身。法爾加島上，康恩丘巴縛海后蒂亞巴爾；其像鑄於盾上，使戰陣中敵力消而己力增。瑪那南之獵犬追逐毀田之豬，悉數亡於後稱犬湖之湖。

sensitivity.note: Manannan mac Lir is the euhemerized sea-god; 'buried standing' is a standard divine-grave motif. The Isle of Man (Emain Ablach / Mannanan's isle) is the traditional symbolic pin for the Island of Falga.

passages.text: As to Manannan the Proud, son of Lir, after he had made places for the rest of the Tuatha de Danaan to live in, he went away out of Ireland himself. Some said he was dead, and got his death by Uillenn Faebarderg of the Red Edge, in battle at Magh Cuilenn; that Manannan was buried standing on his feet, and no sooner was he buried than a great lake burst up under his feet in the place that was a red bog till that time, and the lake got the name of Loch Orbson from one of the names of Manannan. And it was said that red Badb was glad and many women were sorry at that battle. Yet he had many places of living and was often heard of in Ireland after; it was he sent a messenger to Etain, mother of Conaire the High King; it was he brought up Deirdre's children in Emhain of the Apple Trees; and it was he taught Cuchulain the use of the Gae Bulg. Some say Culain the Smith, that gave his name to Cuchulain, was Manannan himself, for he had many shapes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before Culain came to Ulster he was living in the Island of Falga, one of Manannan's places. Conchubar, advised by a Druid, went to ask the smith there to make arms for him, and while he worked Conchubar walked on the strand and saw a sea-woman asleep on the shore. He put bonds on her in her sleep; when she awoke she asked her freedom: "I am Tiabhal, one of the queens of the sea. Bid Culain that is making your shield to put my likeness on it and my name about it, and whenever you go into battle with that shield the strength of your enemies will lessen, and your own strength will increase." Conchubar let her go, and got the victory wherever he brought that shield. And Manannan had good hounds one time, but they hunted a pig that was making a desert of the whole country, and at a lake it turned on them, and no hound of them escaped alive; the pig made for an island named after it, and the lake got the name of Loch Conn, the Lake of the Hounds.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

title.en: Tuag and the Sleep-Spell of Fer Ferdiad
title.zh: 圖雅格與費爾·費爾迪亞德之催眠咒

region.zh: 愛爾蘭格拉斯河口（象徵定位）

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. VIII, eBook #14465

summary.en: Tuag, a fosterling of Conaire the High King, is reared in Tara behind a great company of guardians, to be kept for a king's asking. Manannan sends his pupil, the Druid Fer Ferdiad, in the shape of a woman of the household, who sings a sleep-spell over her and carries her away to Inver Glas; while he looks for a boat a flood-tide wave comes over the girl and drowns her, and Manannan kills Fer Ferdiad in his anger. The wave that drowned Tuag is remembered as one of the three great waves of Ireland.
summary.zh: 圖雅格為百戰王康奈爾之養女，於塔拉被重兵環衛撫養，以待君王求婚。瑪那南遣門徒德魯伊費爾·費爾迪亞德化身侍女，以催眠咒攜其至格拉斯河口；彼尋船之際，漲潮之浪沒圖雅格，她溺亡。瑪那南怒殺費爾·費爾迪亞德。沒頂之浪遂成愛爾蘭三大浪之一。

sensitivity.note: The Wave of Tuag (Tonn Tuaithe) is one of the three great waves of Ireland in the dindsenchas tradition; a failed-elopement etiology. Pin symbolic at the Dublin coast where the tradition locates the strand.

passages.text: There was a young girl of the name of Tuag, a fosterling of Conaire the High King, reared in Teamhair, and a great company of the daughters of the kings of Ireland was put about her, so that she would be kept for a king's asking. But Manannan sent Fer Ferdiad, of the Tuatha de Danaan, that was a pupil of his own and a Druid, in the shape of a woman of his own household, and he went where Tuag was, and sang a sleep-spell over her, and brought her away to Inver Glas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: There he laid her down while he went looking for a boat, that he might bring her away in her sleep to the Land of the Ever-Living Women. But a wave of the flood-tide came over the girl, and she was drowned, and Manannan killed Fer Ferdiad in his anger. It was through Manannan that the wave of Tuag, one of the three great waves of Ireland, got its name.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

region.zh: 愛爾蘭多尼戈爾郡貝利沙納克

texts.period: Late medieval Irish tale tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. IX, eBook #14465

summary.en: At O'Donnell's feast in Ballyshannon a strange clown walks in without passing the gate — old striped clothes, puddle-water splashing in his shoes. He scorns the harpers, plays music sweet enough to sleep women in their pains, refuses clothes and honour, and vanishes in the middle of his music while the watchers strike each other down. Resurrecting them with a herb, he moves from house to house under new names, "one day sweet, another day sour," doing tricks and leaving life restored behind him.
summary.zh: 奧唐奈於貝利沙納克設宴時，一衣衫襤褸之流浪漢不入門而現身，鞋中濺滿泥水。他嘲弄琴師，卻奏出使產婦入睡之美樂；不受衣賞榮銜，樂聲中消失，守衛誤傷彼此倒地。他以草藥救活眾人，四處更名行奇，自言「一日甜，一日酸」，所過之處死而復生。

sensitivity.note: Manannan's wandering-kern cycle is late medieval comedic mythos (the god as beggar-trickster); resurrection tag from the herb that revives the slain. Pin at the feast site named in the tale.

passages.text: Aodh Dubh O'Donnell was holding a feast one time in Bel-atha Senaig, and while they were boasting of the goodness of his house and of his musicians, they saw a clown coming towards them, old striped clothes he had, and puddle water splashing in his shoes, and his sword sticking out naked behind him, and in his hand three spears of hollywood scorched and blackened. When the gate-keeper was brought, he said he had never seen the man before. "Let him off, O'Donnell," said the stranger, "for it was as easy for me to come in as it will be to me to go out again." The musicians began to play their sweetest tunes, but the strange man called out that never was a noise of hammers beating on iron in any bad place so bad to listen to. With that he took a harp and made music that would put women in their pains and wounded men after a battle into a sweet sleep.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.

passages.text: They were afraid he might go from them, and put twenty armed horsemen and twenty men on foot to hold him back; but while they were all listening to his harp, he called out: "Here I am coming, and watch me well now or you will lose me." The watchers lifted their axes in haste and struck at one another till all were stretched in blood. The clown bade the gate-keeper ask twenty cows and a hundred of free land of O'Donnell as a fee, and take an herb and rub it in the mouth of each man, and they would rise up whole and well again. So the gate-keeper did that, and brought all the people to life again. And that is the way Manannan used to be going round Ireland, doing tricks and wonders; if he was put on a gallows itself, he would be found safe in the house after, and some other man on the gallows in his place. But he did no harm, and those that would be put to death by him, he would bring them to life again with a herb out of his bag.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.

title.en: The Thread of Silk and the Hunt in the Air

region.en: Magh Lorg, Co. Monaghan, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭莫納亨郡馬格·洛格（象徵定位）

texts.period: Late medieval Irish tale tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. IX, eBook #14465

summary.en: Calling himself the Gilla Decair, Manannan comes to Tadg O'Cealaigh and for five marks performs tricks: blowing away a middle rush between two fingers, wagging one ear alone, and — greatest of all — casting a thread of silk that fastens to a cloud, up which run a hare, a hound, a serving-boy, and a beautiful girl. When he draws the thread down, the boy is courting the girl and the hound chewing the hare's bones; he strikes the boy's head off, then restores it — but turned backwards — and at Tadg's word twists it straight again.
summary.zh: 自稱「劣僕」的瑪那南到訪塔格·奧基拉，索五馬克表演戲法：兩指間吹走中間燈芯草、單側動耳，最絕者為擲絲線掛於雲端，兔、犬、小僕、美女相繼攀上。收線時，僕正與女調情，犬正嚼兔骨。他怒斬僕首，又復合之——然面朝後；應塔格之言再扭正之。

sensitivity.note: Continuation of the kern cycle; the cloud-thread hunt is a famous shapeshifting-contest episode (compare the pigkeepers' pursuit in cow-raid tradition). Death-and-restoration of the boy tagged 'resurrection' as a staged trick, not a religious miracle.

passages.text: After that he went to where Tadg O'Cealaigh was, having his old striped clothes and his old shoes as before, and when they asked him what art he had he said: "I am good at tricks. And if you will give me five marks I will show you a trick." With that the stranger put three rushes on the palm of his hand: "I will blow away the middle rush now, and the other two will stop as they are." So it was done. He showed too how he could wag the ear on one side of his head and the other would stay still.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he took from his bag a thread of silk and gave a cast of it up into the air, that it was made fast to a cloud. He took a hare out of the same bag and it ran up the thread; then a little dog after the hare, yelping on its track; then a serving-boy after the hound; and out of another bag a beautiful, well-dressed young woman, bidden to follow them and not let the hare be torn by the dog. It was a delight to Tadg to look at them and listen to the hunt going on in the air. But the man of tricks said: "I am afraid there is some bad work going on up there. I am thinking the hound might be eating the hare, and the serving-boy courting the girl." He drew in the thread and found it so, and took his sword and struck the head off the boy; then, taking up the head, made a cast of it at the body, and it joined, but the face was turned backwards — and when Tadg said it would be better for him to be dead than living like that, he took hold of the boy and twisted his head straight, and he was as well as before.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.

title.zh: 基亞班與克莉奧德娜之浪

region.en: Tonn Cliodhna (Glandore strand), Co. Cork, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭科克郡格蘭多爾海濱

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XII, eBook #14465

summary.en: Ciabhan of the Curling Hair, the most beautiful young man of the world, is sent away from the Fianna for jealousy's sake and puts to sea; a rider on a dark grey horse rides under nine waves and rises with the tenth, and carries him to the Land of Promise. There Cliodna of the Fair Hair, who never loved before, gives him her love and sails away with him; but at Teite's Strand treachery plays her asleep with music, a great wave sweeps her off the strand, and the wave that took her bears her name for ever.
summary.zh: 鬈髮之基亞班為世間最美少年，因眾人妒忌而遭芬恩遣離，遂獨舟出海；一騎黑灰馬者潛行九浪、第十浪浮出，引他抵應許之地。彼處從未愛過人的仙姬克莉奧德娜對他一見傾心，隨他乘舟離去；然於泰特海濱，叛者以樂聲使她入睡，巨浪將她捲走。那浪因她得名，永存於世。

sensitivity.note: Tonn Cliodhna at Glandore is one of Ireland's three great waves; the drowning of the fairy bride at the strand is a wave-etiology. Coordinates are the traditional wave site.

passages.text: Ciabhan of the Curling Hair, the king of Ulster's son, was the most beautiful of the young men of the world at that time, but the Fianna grew tired of him because there was not a woman of their women but gave him her love, and Finn had to send him away at the last. He came to the Strand of the Cairn, saw a curragh with a narrow stern of copper, and put out to sea; great white shouting waves rose about him, every one the size of a mountain. Then he saw a rider coming towards him on a dark grey horse having a golden bridle, that would be under the sea for the length of nine waves and would rise with the tenth wave, and no wet on him at all. "What reward would you give to whoever would bring you out of this great danger?" "That you would give your service to whoever would give you his help," said Ciabhan, and he put his hand into the rider's hand, and was drawn on to the horse till they reached the shore of Tir Tairngaire, the Land of Promise.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XII; not verbatim.

passages.text: There was a feast made ready in Manannan's city, and when a clown had done his trick with nine willow rods, he put the rods in Ciabhan's hand, and Ciabhan stood up and did the feat before them all. Gebann, a chief Druid, had a daughter, Cliodna of the Fair Hair, that had never given her love to any man; but when she saw Ciabhan she gave him her love, and agreed to go away with him on the morrow. They went down to the landing-place and got into a curragh, and went on till they came to Teite's Strand in the south of Ireland. Ciabhan came on shore and went looking for deer under the thick branches of the wood, and he left the young girl in the boat on the strand. But the people of Manannan's house came after them having forty ships, and Iuchnu, that was in the curragh with Cliodna, did treachery, and played music to her till she lay down in the boat and fell asleep; and then a great wave came up on the strand and swept her away. And the wave got its name from Cliodna of the Fair Hair, that will be long remembered.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XII; not verbatim.

title.en: Tadg's Voyage to the Lake Island

texts.period: Medieval Irish voyage-tale tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XIV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Tadg son of Cian sails a forty-oxhide curragh to recover his wife and brothers, carried off by the king of Fresen, and is driven through wonder-islands — rams nine-horned as big as horses, birds whose eggs sprout feathers on the eaters — to Inislocha, the Lake Island. There he meets Cesair, first woman of Ireland, now living for ever; Connla of the Red Hair with his fairy bride; and Cliodna of the Fair Hair, who gives him a cup of wine-from-water and a prophecy of his death by a wild deer's wound in the green valley by the Boyne.
summary.zh: 吉安之子塔格乘四十牛皮大舟出海，尋找被弗雷森王擄走的妻子與兄弟；航經奇異群島——角如駿馬之九角公羊、食蛋生羽之奇鳥——終至湖島伊尼斯拉哈。彼處他遇見永生於此的愛爾蘭首位女子塞塞爾、與仙姬相伴的紅髮康拉、以及仙姬克莉奧德娜；她賜他化水為酒之杯，並預言他將死於博因綠谷野鹿之傷。

sensitivity.note: A full immram grafted onto the historical Tadg genealogy (Cian, father of Brian Boru's line); the island sequence is a Census of wonder-islands in the voyage genre. Cross-tradition parallel: voyage over the sea to islands of undying women.

passages.text: Tadg, son of Cian, was going his next heir's round into the west of Munster when Cathmann, king of the country of Fresen, slipped ashore with nine ships and took away Tadg's wife Liban and his two brothers, and put hardship on them — Eoghan to work a common ferry, Airnelach to cut firing, all their food barley seed and muddy water. Tadg escaped by his courage and the use of his sword, and made orders for a curragh that would be fit for a long voyage, with forty ox-hides of hard red leather soaked in bark, and masts and oars and pitch and everything that was wanting, and they put in every sort of meat and drink and clothes that would last a year. They set out over the stormy heavy flood; on they rowed through twenty days and twenty nights till they got sight of a high land, and found it filled with sheep as big as horses, and one great ram of them all had nine horns, and he charged on Tadg's chief men, and Tadg killed him with a lucky cast of his spear that there was no escape from. On two islands after that were flocks of wonderful birds, and when some of the men began eating their eggs, feathers began to grow out on them on the moment, and dropped off again as quick as they came when they went bathing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIV; not verbatim.

passages.text: They came at last to a beautiful inver with green hills about it, and through apple gardens and a plain with a dew of honey over it, with a strong dun on every one of three steep hills. On the nearest hill a white-bodied woman welcomed Tadg: the dun of white marble was the home of the royal line of the kings of Ireland, and this island was Inislocha, the Lake Island. In the middle dun of gold he found Cesair, the first that ever reached Ireland, living for ever since she and the men that were with her came out of that dark unquiet land, and she told him every king and chief man of power in Ireland — Parthalon and Nemed, Firbolgs and Tuatha de Danaan — was in the dun beyond. On the third hill were two comely lovers, a boy and a girl with gold chains about their necks; the boy had a sweet-smelling apple in his hand of which he would eat a third part, and it would never be less, and neither age nor sorrow could touch them that tasted it. "I am son to Conn of the Hundred Battles," he said; "it is Connla I am, and it is this girl of many shapes that brought me here." And Cliodna of the Fair Hair gave Tadg a green cup that turned water to wine, and warned him to keep it from escaping his hand, for at whatever time it escaped him his death would not be far away — a wandering wild deer would wound him in the green valley at the side of the Boinn, and after that strangers would put an end to him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XIV; not verbatim.

title.en: Laeghaire Crimthann's Raid into Magh Mell
title.zh: 萊格爾·克里姆坦遠征幸福平原

region.en: Loch na nEan (Lake of Birds), Co. Galway, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭戈爾韋郡鳥湖（象徵定位）

texts.period: Medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Fiachna of the Sidhe rises from the Lake of Birds to ask mortal help: his wife has been carried off by Goll, king of a people of Magh Mell, the Happy Plain. Laeghaire son of Crimthan Cass goes down into the lake with fifty fighting men, kills Goll in battle, restores the woman to Fiachna, and is rewarded with Fiachna's daughter Deorgreine, a Tear of the Sun, and fifty women for his fifty men — and for a year and a day the Sidhe keep them in the Happy Plain.
summary.zh: 仙族菲亞克納自鳥湖現身，請求凡人相助：其妻被幸福平原之王戈爾擄去。克里姆坦之子萊格爾率五十戰士入湖，陣斬戈爾，將女子歸還菲亞克納，並得菲亞克納之女「太陽之淚」德奧格萊恩為妻，其五十戰士各得一名仙女，眾人在幸福平原留居一年又一日。

sensitivity.note: A mortal raid into the underwater otherworld (descent-underworld by way of a lake); the sithchean (year and a day) elapsed among the Sidhe marks the otherworld-time motif. Lake pin symbolic; Magh Mell has no earthly coordinates.

passages.text: Laeghaire, son of the King of Connacht, Crimthan Cass, was out one day with his father near Loch na-n Ean, the Lake of Birds, and they saw a man coming to them through the mist, with long golden-yellow hair streaming after him, a gold-hilted sword at his belt, two five-barbed darts in his hand, and a five-folded crimson cloak about his shoulders. "I am come to look for the help of fighting men," said the stranger; "my name is Fiachna, son of Betach, of the men of the Sidhe; my wife was taken from my pillow and brought away by Eochaid, son of Sal; I killed him, and now she is gone to a brother's son of his, Goll, son of Dalbh, king of a people of Magh Mell. Seven battles I gave him, but they all went against me, and on this very day there is another to be fought, and I am come to ask help."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Fiachna went down into the lake, for it was out of it he had come, and Laegaire went down into it after him, fifty fighting men along with him. They saw a strong place before them and a company of armed men, and Goll, son of Dalbh, at the head of them. The two fifties attacked one another, and Goll fell, but Laeghaire and his fifty made a great slaughter of their enemies, so that not one of them made his escape. Laeghaire and his men went on to the dun of Magh Mell, and he called out to the men about it: "Your king has got his death, your chief men have fallen, let the woman come out, and I will give you your own lives." They agreed to that, and brought the woman out, and she made a complaint that got the name of "The Lament of the Daughter of Eochaid the Dumb." And that night Fiachna's daughter, Deorgreine, a Tear of the Sun, was given to Laeghaire as his wife, and fifty other women were given to his fifty fighting men, and they stopped with them there to the end of a year.
